newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico brewers to benefit from price rise-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Mexico brewers to benefit from price rise-analysts.

text.p: A move by Fomento Economico Mexicano SA (FEMSA) to increase beer prices by 22 percent was welcomed on Tuesday by analysts, who said higher prices would likely boost profitability for both of Mexico's brewers.
FEMSA's beer division, Cerveceria Cuauhtemoc Moctezuma, announced on Monday that it had raised beer prices to retailers by 22 percent. The prices are expected to hit consumers in about a month.

The increase is likely to be the first real price increase in several years because many economists see inflation running about 18 percent in 1997. The Mexican government has set a 1997 goal of 15 percent inflation.
Grupo Modelo, FEMSA's chief competitor in the Mexican beer market, is widely expected to raise its prices by the same 22 percent, with an announcement probably coming next week, analysts said.
In the past two years, both companies set price increases that lagged inflation, largely because the economic crisis of 1995 devastated the buying power of millions of Mexicans.
"A real price increase had to come at some time, so why not when they see a recovery under way?" Laura Ehlrich, a food and beverage analyst with Paribas in New York, told Reuters. "It makes sense."
Ehrlich said she believed the Mexican market would absorb the higher prices, with growth in sales volumes slowing only a bit in 1997.
The companies think any slowdown in sales volume growth will be offset by the higher prices, meaning revenues will not decrease, she said.
"It's very positive for both of them," said Marco Vera, a Mexico City-based analyst with Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "Prices had lagged so much that I don't expect this to impact volumes."

Another New York-based analyst said the move by FEMSA has eased market fears of a possible price war between Modelo and FEMSA when Modelo's brewery in the north-central state of Zacatecas comes on line this year, increasing beer supply.
Instead, FEMSA and Modelo are confident that Mexican beer drinkers finally have recovered enough from the crisis to take on real price increases.

"That's clearly what they're thinking," said the analyst, who asked not to be identified. "In the worst-case scenario, if the market does not absorb the new price increases, then next year's price increase won't be as high compared to inflation."
